name: Umayyad Caliphate

territory.border: hb:700:Umayyad Caliphate + hb:700:Barghawata + hb:700:Mauri + hb:700:Aures + hb:700:Warsenis + hb:700:Sasanian Empire + hb:700:Hejaz + hb:700:Kingdom of Sind + hb:700:Kwarezm

areaKm2.note: Wikipedia infobox gives 11.1-15 million km2 for 720 (Taagepera 1997 low, Blankinship 1994 p. 37 "five million square miles" high). Seshat codes 9.0 million km2 for 700 (https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/131, low). The world_700 union in border measures only 5.82 million km2 on the sphere, because that file still shows Iran as Sasanian (used here as the conquered Iranian plateau) and leaves interior Arabia and Transoxiana unnamed.

population.note: Seshat codes 23-33 million for 700 CE. Cross-check: HYDE/Gapminder country series (OWID) for 700 sum to ~35-40 million over Iberia, the Maghreb, Egypt, the Levant, Iraq, Iran, Arabia, Transoxiana and Sind, but Sind and Transoxiana were only partly held. Mid = Seshat midpoint.

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Garrison cities (amsar) Kufa, Basra, Fustat, Kairouan and Wasit plus Damascus, Alexandria and Merv; Seshat puts the largest settlement at 200,000-400,000. Far above contemporary Latin Europe.

activePersonnel.note: Muqatila on the salaried diwan register: ~300,000 in 700 (Kennedy, Armies of the Caliphs, 2001, p. 20), 400,000 under Hisham (Blankinship 1994); Blankinship gives Syria 175,000, Jazira 75,000, Khurasan 54,000, Egypt 40,000, North Africa, Spain and Sind 30,000+ each. Registers counted many who drew pay but rarely campaigned, so the effective field force was smaller (see notes).

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess. Non-registered Arab tribesmen, mawali auxiliaries, Berber and Sogdian levies callable for a campaign season.

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess. Navy crews of the Egyptian, Syrian and Ifriqiyan fleets (~200 galleys x ~100-150 men, largely Coptic and Syrian Christian rowers), plus diwan clerks and engineers.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. The diwan already enrolled ~1% of the population; a general call of all Arab settlers plus converts could add perhaps half again.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Educated guess. Kennedy stresses that Umayyad armies, especially the Syrian ahl al-Sham, fought mostly as close-order spear infantry with cavalry on the wings. Share of the diwan total.

quality.note: Rubric quality 0.5-0.75: mail-armoured Syrian infantry with spears and swords, era-typical to good.

training.note: Rubric training 0.5-0.75: salaried regular troops, Syrian army campaigning yearly against Byzantium.

count.note: Educated guess. Foot archers, a standard component of Umayyad armies (Kennedy 2001 ch. on organisation). Share of the diwan total.
Educated guess. Berber and Arab tribal irregulars.
Educated guess. Mail-armoured lancers of the Syrian and Khurasani armies. Share of the diwan total.

quality.note: Rubric 0.75: good Arabian horses, mail; no stirrup-based shock tactics yet.

count.note: Educated guess. Arab tribal and Berber light horse, Khurasani mounted archers.
Educated guess. Traction trebuchets (manjaniq): five were used against Mecca in 692 and the great "al-Arus" engine at Daybul in 711. Empire-wide count unknown.

Educated guess. War galleys of the Syrian, Egyptian and Ifriqiyan fleets after the losses at Constantinople 717-718. Theophanes gives 1,800 ships for the 717 armada and Egypt and Africa sent 400 and 360 ships in 718 (chronicle figures, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Constantinople_(717%E2%80%93718)); those include transports.

quality.note: Rubric 0.5: dromon-type galleys, no answer to Greek fire.

count.note: Educated guess. Smaller galleys and river craft on the Nile, Tigris and Euphrates.

commandQuality.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: proven conquest generals (Qutayba, Maslama, Muhammad ibn Qasim) but the 717-718 siege of Constantinople ended in disaster.

cohesion.note: Rubric 0.5: regular units with regional (jund) identity, undermined by the Qays-Yaman tribal feud.

morale.note: Rubric 0.5: just repulsed at Constantinople (718); frontiers stalling (Blankinship, End of the Jihad State).

weapons.note: Anchor 3 (iron weapons, torsion artillery) to 4 (crossbow, trebuchet): composite bows, lances, traction trebuchets; no counterweight trebuchet yet.

armor.note: Anchor 3 (mail): mail and lamellar for regulars.

ships.note: Anchor 3 (galleys): dromon-type galleys built in Alexandria, Acre and Tunis arsenals.

fortification.note: Anchor 3: inherited Roman and Sasanian walled cities; ribat forts.

logistics.note: Anchor 3 (engineered roads, depot system) to 4: camel trains, amsar depots and the diwan pay system.

communications.note: Anchor 3 (mounted relay posts): the barid relay post reorganised by Mu'awiya and Abd al-Malik.

isr.note: Anchor 3 by year (classical scouting and spies).

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project 2023 (via OWID): Egypt 730 = 1,164, Iraq 730 = 1,466 (2011 int$). Iberia, the Maghreb and Iran probably lower; mid ~1,200.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. Diwan stipends were the largest item of state spending (Kennedy 2001); with taxes perhaps 8-12% of output, the army took roughly half.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. Textiles, metalwork, papyrus and shipbuilding in an agrarian economy.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Egypt and the Sawad of Iraq fed large garrison cities.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in a pre-modern age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model as the classical snapshots; medieval age structures were similar (high mortality, young population).

roadKm.note: Educated guess. Inherited Roman roads in Syria, Egypt and North Africa and Sasanian roads in Iran; Khurasan road and pilgrim routes.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess. Alexandria, Acre, Tyre, Tripoli, Tunis, Basra, Clysma, Ceuta and others.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. Mediterranean and Indian Ocean (Basra-Sind) shipping; no count exists.

supplyRangeKm.note: Engels (isbn:0520042727, ch. 1) for pre-modern armies with pack animals, scaled up for camel trains that let Arab armies cross desert gaps (Kennedy 2001).

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. ~0.05-0.15 camels, horses, mules and oxen per inhabitant.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.1 (familiar terrain, local supply) to 1.2 (walled cities); the desert depth around Syria and Iraq favours the defender, but most subjects were non-Muslim and not reliably supportive.

notes: Snapshot = 720 CE, after Umar II and before the 720s-730s frontier disasters (Day of Thirst 724, Tours 732, Berber revolt 740). Army size rests on diwan registers: Kennedy (Armies of the Caliphs, 2001, p. 20) ~300,000 enrolled c. 700, Blankinship (End of the Jihad State, 1994) 400,000 under Hisham, both via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayyad_Caliphate; registers overstate the deployable force, and campaign armies were 10,000-40,000. Chronicle figures for the 717 armada (Michael the Syrian 200,000 men, 5,000 ships; al-Mas'udi 120,000) are rejected. Population convention: everything inside the caliph's direct rule, Iberia to Sind and Transoxiana; tributary Armenian and Georgian princes excluded. Border is a union of world_700 features (see area note) and is far too small; prefer the areaKm2 value. Force split among roles is an educated division of the register total.
